stories.text:
Noah found a big mud puddle. It was round and brown. She put on her red hat. She said, "I will race to the puddle."

Her friend Ben said, "You will get muddy."

Noah said, "That is the fun part."

She ran fast. Splash! Her boots got wet. The mud was soft like pudding. She made little mud pies.

Then she looked up. On the far side of the playground, she saw the green light. It was bright as a new leaf. It sat on the fence. It was sunny and warm.

"Come see my pies," said Ben.

Noah turned back. "Look at the green light," she said.

"I see it," said Ben. "It is just a light."

Noah played more. She jumped in the puddle. But her eyes went to the green light again. It was small and far. She could not touch it.

The sun went down. Her mom called, "Time to go."

Noah waved to the puddle. She waved to the green light. It stayed on the fence. She went home with muddy hands.

stories.text: Noah found a big mud puddle on the playground. She put on her red hat. "Watch me jump," she said. She jumped in with both feet. Splash! Mud went on her socks. She laughed. "Again!" said her friend Max. They had a race to the puddle. Noah won. She was little but fast. The puddle felt squishy and cool. Then Noah looked up. Then she looked again. The green light was still there, far past the swings. "Do you see that?" she asked. "See what?" said Max. Noah didn't answer. She ran to the puddle once more. But she kept turning her head. The green light sat on the far side, bright as a new leaf. It never came closer. "Noah, you're not playing," said Max. "I am," she said. But she wasn't. She watched the green light until her mom called her home for dinner.

Noah found a big mud puddle on the playground path. It was round and brown and perfect. She put on her hat. She stepped in with both boots.

“Watch me!” she said.

Her boots went splash. The mud made a little lake. Noah wanted to race her friend Ben to the far side. But then she saw the green light.

It sat on the far side of the playground. It was bright as a new leaf. The sun made it shine.

“Come on, Noah!” said Ben.

Noah took one step. The green light blinked. She took another step. The green light glowed. She forgot the mud puddle. She forgot the race. She forgot her hat.

“Noah, you said you would race!”

She heard him, but her feet turned the other way. The green light was so bright. It was bright as a new leaf.

“Noah!”

The green light. The green light. She wanted it. She wanted the green light.

Ben pulled her hand. “It is just a puddle,” he said.

Noah looked down. Her boots were muddy. The green light stayed far away. She sighed. Then she splashed Ben.

Noah liked to splash in the mud puddle. She put on her hat. She ran a little race to the puddle. Splash! The mud was soft and brown.

Then she saw the green light. It was on the far side of the playground. It was bright as a new leaf.

"Come play," said her friend.

Noah did not hear. She looked at the green light.

"Noah, look at my mud pie."

Noah did not look. She wanted the green light.

The sun was warm. The puddle was right there. But Noah walked away.

"Where are you going?" said her friend.

Noah did not answer. She walked to the far side of the playground. The green light stayed far away.

She reached out. The green light was still far away.

"Come back," said her friend.

Noah shook her head. She wanted the green light. She wanted the green light. She wanted the green light.

The mud puddle dried up in the sun. Noah did not splash. She just stood there. She looked at the green light. The green light was bright as a new leaf. And it was always, always too far.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: under a door down the hall
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The kitten was named Ella, and she loved the piano. On rainy evenings she sat on the bench and tapped the keys with her fuzzy paws. Plink, plink, plonk. She did not know the song, but she liked it.

The rain went tap, tap on the window. Ella stopped. Down the hall, under a door, she saw the green light. It was round like a marble. It made a soft glow on the floor. She left the piano and walked to it.

She put one paw in her pocket. Nothing was there. She tried to shake the door, but it did not move. The green light stayed on the other side.

Ella went back to the piano. She tapped one key. Then she heard a tiny sound. A mouse was hiding inside the piano. The green light was just the moon. So Ella played, and the mouse stayed, and the rain kept falling.

stories.text:
The kitten walked on the piano keys. Plink, plonk, plink. Ella laughed and clapped her hands. The rain tapped the window. It was a rainy evening.

Ella put a fuzzy blanket in her pocket. She wanted the kitten to nap. But the kitten jumped down. It ran to the hall.

Ella saw a green light under a door down the hall. The green light was round like a marble. It glowed on the floor. Ella wanted to touch the green light. She reached for it. The green light stayed under the door. She could not have it.

She sat by the door. The green light made a small circle. She tried to shake the door. It did not open. The green light did not come to her.

Then the kitten meowed. It was behind her, not past the door. The green light was just a night lamp in the baby's room. Ella picked up the kitten. She held it close.

The green light still glowed. But Ella did not reach for it. She went back to the piano. The kitten walked on the keys again. Plink, plonk, plink.

stories.text:
The kitten walked on the piano keys. Ella laughed. Plink, plunk, plink! The kitten was soft and fuzzy. Rain tapped the window. It was a rainy evening.

The green light kept glowing under the door. Round like a marble. It was still there.

Ella played one soft note. Then she played another. The green light shone and shone. She could not have it. But she could have the song.

She reached for the green light. Her paw found only a pocket of cold air. She gave a little shake. The green light did not move.

Back at the piano, she tried a song. But her eyes kept turning to the hall. The green light called her again. She went back. She reached. She could not touch it.

The rain kept falling. The green light kept shining. Ella sat by the door and watched the green light.

Then the door opened. It was just the moon in a puddle. The green light was only that.

Ella went back to the piano. She played one sad note.

stories.topic: A fire truck and a kitten
stories.name: Lena

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
In the hot summer day, Lena saw a fire truck go down the street. It was big and red. It made a loud noise. Lena waved at it.

Lena sat on the hill with her kitten, Pip. Pip was small and soft. The sun was very hot. Lena wanted to swim in cold water. She wanted something icy to drink.

Pip did not like the heat. Pip hid under a bush. Lena looked for Pip. She saw something in the sky. It was very low. It was a green light. It was glowing like a lantern. Lena did not know what it was. She wanted to touch it. But it was too far away. She looked back at the bush.

Then Pip jumped out. Pip was not under the bush. Pip was on the fire truck! The fire truck had stopped. A kind firefighter held Pip. Lena laughed. She got her kitten back. The green light stayed in the sky.

stories.text:
In the hot summer day, Lena saw a fire truck stop by the hill. A tiny kitten was stuck up in a tree. The fire truck came to help the kitten get down. Lena watched the firemen climb up. They were very kind.

Then Lena looked up. Very low in the sky, she saw the green light. It was glowing like a lantern. It made her feel quiet inside. She wished she could touch it.

The firemen brought the kitten down safe. Lena clapped her hands. She wanted to give the kitten some icy water. But the kitten did not want to swim in a bowl. It just wanted to nap.

Lena sat on the hill. She looked at the green light again. It was still glowing like a lantern. She felt a small pull in her heart.

Then the kitten climbed into Lena's lap. It purred and purred. The twist was that the kitten was not scared at all. It had just wanted a friend. Lena smiled and held it close.

It was a hot summer day, and Lena sat on the hill to watch the fire truck. The big red truck came down the street with a loud siren. Firefighters jumped out to help a kitten stuck in a tree. Lena clapped her hands. The kitten was small and scared.

Then Lena saw the green light in the sky. It was very low and glowing like a lantern. "Green light," she whispered. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to swim up to it. But it was too far.

The firefighters got the kitten down. The kitten ran to Lena. She held it close. "Green light," she said again. She looked up. The green light was still there, glowing like a lantern.

Lena wanted an icy drink. She wanted the green light. She held the kitten and watched the green light. The green light did not move. It just glowed.

Then the kitten licked her hand. Lena laughed. The green light blinked once, like a tiny star, and faded away. The kitten was warm. That was enough.

In the hot summer day, Lena watched the fire truck zoom down the street. A tiny kitten sat on the sidewalk, mewing loud. The fire truck stopped. Firefighters jumped out. One picked up the kitten. Lena clapped.

Then she saw the green light in the sky, very low, glowing like a lantern. Her heart pulled. She wanted to touch it. The green light was so close. She forgot the fire truck. She forgot the kitten.

“Come on,” she whispered. She ran up the hill. She tried to swim through the hot air. It felt thick. She wanted an icy drink, but she only wanted the green light.

The green light glowed like a lantern. She reached out. It stayed just ahead. She thought, green light, green light, green light. Nothing else mattered.

Then the kitten mewed again. Lena looked down. The kitten had followed her up the hill. It was thirsty. Lena gave it water from her bottle.

The green light blinked and rose higher. It was a firefly all along. Lena smiled and petted the kitten. The green light still glowed, but now she had a friend.

I like the fire truck. It is big and red. It goes wee-woo! down the street. Lena runs to see it. A tiny kitten sits on the truck.

Then Lena sees the green light. The green light is low in the sky. It glows like a lantern. The green light, the green light. She wants the green light. She forgets the kitten.

The day is hot. Lena climbs a hill to get the green light. The green light stays far away. She wants to swim in the sky and touch it. She wants an icy drink, but she wants the green light more. Green light, green light.

The kitten mews. Lena does not hear. Green light, green light, green light.

Then the kitten jumps on her head. Lena blinks. The green light was the fire truck's little lamp all along. It was not in the sky. It was on the truck. Lena laughs. She holds the kitten. The green light can wait.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: in a tent across the camp
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Ella found a squirrel's stash under the big oak tree. Acorns, shiny and brown, sat in a tidy pile. She wanted to keep them. But they were not hers.

She tried to dig a new hole for her own nuts. The dirt was hard. Her little hands got tired. This was a problem.

Ella sat back. She thought and thought. Then she had an idea. She would not take the stash. She would make her own.

She gathered three acorns from the grass. She dug a soft spot by the fence. She dropped them in and covered them up. She felt proud.

Just before bedtime, she looked across the camp. In a tent far away, a green light flickered on and off. It blinked like a tiny star. Then it went dark.

Ella yawned. Her own little stash was safe. She would check it in the morning. She closed her eyes and slept.

stories.name: Ella

stories.text:
Little Ella found a squirrel's stash. She saw nuts under the big tree. She wanted to keep them. But they were not hers. That was her little problem.

She sat by her tent. Just before bedtime, she saw a green light. It was in a tent across the camp. The green light flickered on and off. Ella watched it. She turned back to the nuts.

She could dig a hole. She could hide the nuts for later. But the squirrel worked hard. Ella felt bad.

The green light flickered again. On. Off. It pulled at her. She looked away.

She put the nuts back under the tree. The squirrel came down. It took one nut. Then another. Ella felt proud.

She did not need the stash. The green light blinked across the camp. On. Off. She did not need that either. She zipped her tent and went to bed.

stories.name: Ella

stories.text:
Little Ella hid acorns under the big tree. She had one small problem. Her pile kept falling over. So Ella made a plan. She would dig a deep hole. Then she would put the acorns inside.

Just before bedtime, she saw the green light. It was in a tent across the camp. The green light flickered on and off. Ella turned back to her hole. She dug and dug. The green light flickered again. She looked up. The green light was so far away.

Ella put the acorns in the hole. She felt proud. But the green light flickered once more. She wanted to go to it. She could not. It was across the camp. The green light blinked and blinked.

Ella patted the dirt down. Her stash was safe. She looked at the tent one last time. The green light flickered on and off. Then she went to bed. Her little problem was solved.

stories.name: Ella

stories.text:
Little Ella hid nuts under the big tree. She wanted a good stash for winter. She dug a hole with her small paws. She felt proud.

Then a problem came. Her hole was too small. The nuts kept rolling out. Ella pushed them back. They rolled away again.

Just before bedtime, she saw the green light. It was in a tent across the camp. The green light flickered on and off. On and off. Ella watched the green light. She wanted it. She reached for it. She could not have it.

The green light flickered on and off.

She turned back to her hole. She dug it deeper. She made it wide. The nuts stayed in. Her stash was safe.

But the green light flickered on and off. Ella looked at the green light again. She wanted the green light so much. The green light, the green light, the green light.

Then she yawned. She curled up by her tree. Her stash was full. She was proud. The green light flickered on and off, far away, without her.

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Ella hid nuts under the big tree. She would dig and dig. Her cheeks got puffy. She felt so proud.

Then Ella saw it. Across the camp, in a tent, a green light flickered on and off. Green light. Green light. Her nuts did not matter.

She ran to the tent flap. The green light flickered on and off. She reached a paw out. She could not touch it. Green light. Green light. She wanted it so much.

Her stash sat alone under the tree. The dark came. The green light flickered on and off. Green light. Green light. Nothing else was real.

Then Mama found her. Mama said, "Your nuts will get wet." That was a little problem.

Ella turned away. She dug fast. She piled the nuts in a safe, dry place. She felt proud again.

The green light still flickered on and off across the camp. Ella looked once. Then she went to bed.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Mud squished under Theo the turtle as he crawled to the tide pool. The storm made the sky dark. Waves splashed over the rocks. "I want to find a crab," Theo said.

His friend Max the mouse held a tiny glove. "The wind is strong," Max said. "Hold my glove so you do not blow away."

Theo held the glove. He saw a wiggly crab near a stack of stones. The crab waved one claw. Then it hid.

Rain fell hard. Theo and Max sat by the pool. The water rose and fell.

In the dark of the woods, far away, Theo saw a green light. It was faint as a star. The green light blinked between the trees. Theo reached one slow foot toward it. He could not touch it.

"The green light is too far," Max said.

"I know," said Theo. "But I like to look."

The storm went away. The tide pool was calm. Theo watched the green light until it faded. Then he crawled home with Max.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Mornings were for the tide pool. Theo was a small turtle with a slow, happy walk. He loved the pool by the rocks. The water was cold and clear. A crab waved a wiggly claw. A starfish held on like a glove. Theo could watch it all day.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain came down. The storm pushed the sea up high. The pool filled with foam and ran away. Theo felt sad.

"Come with me," said his friend Pip. "The woods are dry."

They walked under the trees. The storm made the woods dark. Then Theo saw it. A green light, faint as a star, far between the trunks. It was just a green light. It did not move. It did not come closer.

"Can we go there?" Theo asked.

"No," said Pip. "That is just a green light."

Theo stacked one stone on another to climb. The stack fell down. The green light stayed far away. He reached and reached. His small arms shook.

"Come back," said Pip. "The pool is calm now."

Theo looked once more at the green light. Then he followed Pip home. The tide pool waited. That was enough.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Mud dripped from Theo's shell as he crept to the tide pool. He was a turtle and he loved this small sea. The water was warm and wiggly with crabs. A storm pushed gray clouds overhead.

Theo saw something in the dark of the woods. A green light. It was faint as a star. It blinked between the trees. He wanted it.

"Theo, come back," said his friend Rosa. "The tide pool is here."

But the green light pulled him. He walked past a lost glove in the mud. He climbed a stack of wet rocks. The green light stayed far away.

"Please," Theo said. "I just want to touch it."

"You can't," Rosa said. "It is only a shine. Stay with me."

The storm rumbled. Rain fell fast. The green light was still faint as a star.

Theo reached one more time. His foot slipped. Rosa caught him.

"Let it go," she said. "The pool needs you."

Theo looked back at the green light. Then he turned to the warm little sea.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Mud squished under Theo the turtle as he crawled to the tide pool. The storm made the waves splash high. He wanted to sit in the pool and feel the calm water.

Then he saw the green light.

It was in the dark of the woods, past the rocks. It looked faint as a star. Theo forgot the tide pool. He turned toward the green light.

His friend Rosa the crab waved a claw. "Theo! The pool is this way!"

"I want the green light," Theo said.

"You can't go in the woods," said Rosa. "Here, take my glove. The rocks are wiggly."

Theo put on the glove. He tried to stack three stones to climb. They fell down.

The green light blinked far away. Theo reached and reached. The tide pool waited, but he did not go back.

"Please stay," Rosa said.

Theo watched the green light until the sky went gray. He never touched it.

stories.topic: a turtle and a tide pool
stories.name: Theo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
My turtle Theo found a tide pool. He sat in the wiggly water and watched the small crabs. Then he saw the green light. It was in the dark of the woods. It was faint as a star.

"Come back," said his friend Bea. "The storm is coming."

Theo did not come back. He walked toward the green light. Rain fell on his shell. The wind blew his little glove away. He did not care.

"The green light," said Theo.

"It is just a light," said Bea.

Theo climbed a stack of wet rocks. He reached for the green light. The green light was far away.

"Green light," said Theo. "Green light."

The storm shook the trees. Bea held his foot. Theo still reached.

"Green light," said Theo. "Green light. Green light."

The green light did not come closer. It only blinked, faint as a star. Theo reached and reached. The green light stayed in the dark of the woods, and Theo could not have it.

features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carl the owl sat on a branch and watched the moon. The moon was big and white. Carl loved the moon. But a storm came. The wind blew hard. The rain fell fast. The moon hid behind dark clouds. Carl was sad.

Carl sat on a chair by his tree. He wanted the moon back. He felt shy and small. He did not like the storm. Then Carl saw a green light at the very top of a tall tree. The green light shimmered like water in the rain. Carl blinked. The green light was pretty. But Carl wanted the moon.

Carl said, "I will run to the top tree." He flew up and up. The wind pushed him. But he did not stop. Then the clouds moved away. The moon came back! It was bright and round. Carl smiled. He sat on his branch and looked at the moon. The storm was gone. Carl was happy.

stories.text:
Cuddled in his chair, Ben the owl watched the moon. It was a stormy afternoon. The wind blew hard. Rain tapped the window.

Ben wanted to see the moon. But clouds hid it. He felt shy and small. He could not fly in the rain. His wings would get wet.

Then Ben saw a small green light at the very top of a tall tree. It shimmered like water. The green light was far away. Ben wished he could reach it.

He tried to run to the tree. But owls do not run well. He slipped on wet leaves. "Oh no," said Ben.

He had a little problem. He needed help. His friend Mia the mouse came. "I will help," she said. Mia climbed the tree. She did not need to fly.

Mia brought back a soft leaf. The leaf was dry. Ben smiled. The rain stopped. The clouds went away.

The moon came out. It was big and bright. Ben saw the green light again. It shimmered like water. But now Ben was happy. He had his chair and his friend. The green light could stay in the tree.

stories.text:
Close by the barn, Ben the owl sat on a wooden chair. He wanted to see the moon. But the afternoon was dark with storm clouds. Rain went tap tap on the roof.

Ben flew to a tall tree. At the very top, he saw a green light. It shimmered like water. The green light was far away. Ben wanted to touch it. He was shy, so he did not call out. He just looked and looked.

The wind blew hard. Ben felt small. He wanted the moon, but the clouds hid it. He wanted the green light, but it stayed far. He did not run. He sat still.

Then the storm went away. The sky turned soft and blue. Ben saw the moon! It was big and round. It made the green light shine more. The green light shimmered like water on the leaves.

Ben was happy. He did not need to touch it. He just liked to see it. He sat on his chair and smiled at the moon.

stories.text:
Carefully, Ben the owl watched the moon from his little chair. The moon was big and round. But a storm came. Clouds hid the moon. Ben felt sad. He wanted to see the moon again.

Then Ben saw a green light. It was at the very top of a tall tree. The green light was shimmering like water. Ben wanted the green light. He could not reach it. The green light was too high.

Ben did not want the moon now. He only wanted the green light. He flew up. The wind pushed him. He did not stop. He felt shy and small. But he did not want to run away.

The green light stayed far. It shimmered and danced. Ben said, green light. Green light. Green light.

Then the storm stopped. The clouds went away. The moon came back. It was bright and kind. Ben sat in his chair again. He looked at the moon. The green light was still there. But Ben was happy with the moon. That was enough.

Ben felt shy. He hid under a leaf. Then he saw the moon peek out. The moon was soft and white. The moon was not the green light.

Ben tried to run to the moon. Owls do not run. He flopped.

A little problem! His wing hurt. He sat still.

The storm stopped. The moon came out big and round. Ben forgot the green light for a moment.

He hopped home to his chair. Mama Owl hugged him. The moon shone on the window.

Ben smiled. The moon was his. The green light stayed far away, shimmering like water at the very top of the tall tree.

But Ben was happy. The moon was enough.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Winter blew hard and made a blizzard. Jack was glad he had a warm blanket. It was just before bedtime. He pulled the blanket to his chin.

"Stay warm," said Mom. She put a cap on his head. Jack gave a happy roll in the blanket. He was as busy as a bear in a cozy den.

Then Jack saw the green light at the top of the stairs. It was dim, like a sleepy eye. He wanted to touch it. He reached one hand out. The blanket slipped.

"Lie down, Jack," said Mom.

He pulled the blanket back up. The green light blinked once, then went away. Jack did not need it. He had his warm blanket.

"Good night," said Mom.

"Good night," said Jack. He closed his eyes. The snow sang soft on the window, and Jack felt warm and safe.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the top of the stairs

stories.text:
Winter blew hard. Jack was glad for his warm blanket. Snow made a big drifts. The blizzard shook the windows. Jack put on his cap. He was warm and snug. Then he saw the green light at the top of the stairs. It was dim, like a sleepy eye. It was just before bedtime.

"Mom, why is the green light on?" Jack asked.

"It is always on," she said. "It is busy keeping the dark away."

Jack wanted the green light. He did not want to roll out of bed. He pulled his blanket up to his chin. The green light glowed at the top of the stairs. He reached for it with his eyes. He could not touch it.

"Time to sleep," Mom said.

Jack closed his eyes. The blizzard was loud. His blanket was soft. The green light stayed at the top of the stairs, far away. But he had his warm blanket, and he felt safe. He smiled and slept.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

stories.text:
Winter blew hard. Snow piled up past the window. Jack pulled his warm blanket to his chin. It was a blizzard outside. Inside, he was snug.

"Time for bed," said Mom. She put a soft cap on his head.

Jack did not want to sleep. He wanted to roll on the rug. He was too busy for bed.

Then he saw the green light. It glowed at the top of the stairs. It was dim, like a sleepy eye. The green light seemed to call him.

"Mom, what is that green light?" Jack asked.

"Just the night light," she said. "It watches over you."

Jack climbed the stairs. The green light stayed dim. He reached for it. His hand found only air. He could not touch the green light.

"Goodnight, green light," Jack whispered.

He crawled under his warm blanket. The blizzard roared. But Jack felt safe. The green light blinked once, like a slow wink. Jack smiled and closed his eyes.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

stories.text:
When the snow came, Jack pulled the warm blanket up to his chin. The blizzard tapped the window. The house felt safe and small.

"Time for bed," Dad said. "Where is your cap?"

Jack looked for his cap. He was too busy watching the snow. It did a slow roll down the glass.

Then he saw the green light at the top of the stairs. It was dim, like a sleepy eye. It called to him. He wanted to climb up and touch it.

"Jack?" Dad said.

Jack took one step. The green light glowed soft and far. He reached for it. His hand found only air. The green light stayed where it was. He could not have it.

"Come back, buddy. The blanket is warm."

Jack went back. Dad tucked the warm blanket around him. The blizzard roared, but Jack was cozy.

"Goodnight, Jack."

"Goodnight, Dad."

He closed his eyes. The green light waited at the top of the stairs, but Jack did not need it. He had the warm blanket, and he was happy.

Jack reached for the green light. He could not touch it. The green light stayed at the top of the stairs.

Jack wanted the green light. He wanted it so much. The green light, the green light, the green light.

The warm blanket was soft. Mom put it on him. Jack still looked at the green light. The green light did not come closer.

"Goodnight," said Mom.

Jack closed his eyes. The green light was still there. He could not have it. But the blanket was warm. And that was good.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Mama said today was the day. Gus the baby bird would fly. He sat in the nest and looked down. The ground was far. His wings felt small.

"Just try," said his friend Pip the mouse. "I will cheer for you."

Gus hopped to the edge. He flapped once. He flapped twice. Then he fell, soft as a fluffy snowflake, into a snowy bush. He was okay!

Pip ran to him. "You flew a little!"

Gus wanted to try again. But the snow was deep. The wind was cold. They found a tent by the path and hid inside.

Through the tent flap, Gus saw something far away. At the back of a dark shop, past the bare trees, a green light was glittering through the leaves. It shone like a tiny star. Gus did not know what it was. He only knew it was pretty.

"Come on," said Pip. "One more try."

Gus climbed a low branch. He peeked at the sky. He flapped and flapped. This time he stayed up! He flew all the way to the shop door. Pip clapped.

The green light twinkled above him. Gus was happy. He had flown.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Mama said today was the day. Gus was a baby bird. He had fluffy wings. He was scared to fly.

Gus hopped to the edge of the nest. He did not jump. He peeked down at the ground. It looked far away.

A friend came by. It was Sam the snail. "You can do it, Gus," said Sam.

Gus tried again. He flapped his fluffy wings. Then he saw it. At the back of a dark shop, a green light was glittering through the leaves. It was a snowy day. The green light looked warm. Gus wanted to reach the green light.

"Fly to me," said Sam.

Gus looked at the green light. He looked at Sam. He took a breath. Then he jumped. His wings went up and down. He flew!

He did not reach the green light. But he flew to Sam. They sat under a tent of soft snow. Gus was happy. He could fly now. The green light glittered far away.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Mama said today Gus would fly. Gus was a fluffy baby bird. He lived in a nest in a tall tree. His wings felt small. His heart felt big and scared.

"Just jump," said his friend Pip. Pip was a squirrel. "I will catch you."

Gus looked down. Then he saw it. At the back of a dark shop, a green light was glittering through the leaves. It was pretty. It was far away.

"Fly to me," chirped Gus. But the green light did not move.

Gus tried to peek over the nest. He wobbled. He fell. He flapped once, twice, three times. He flew!

But he did not fly to the ground. He flew toward the green light. Pip ran after him. "Wait, Gus!"

The snow fell soft and white. Gus landed on a tent by the shop. The green light was still far. It was always far.

Pip climbed up. "You flew, Gus. That is what matters."

Gus looked at the green light one more time. Then he looked at Pip. He was happy. He was warm. The green light could wait.

stories.name: Gus

stories.text:
Mom said today was the day Gus would fly. Gus was a fluffy baby bird. He stood on the branch and flapped his wings.

Then he saw the green light. It was at the back of a dark shop. The green light was glittering through the leaves.

“Come fly,” said Mom.

But Gus looked at the green light. The green light was so pretty. He wanted the green light.

“Come fly,” said his friend Pip.

Gus hopped once. He looked back. The green light was still glittering through the leaves.

“Fly to me,” said Pip.

Gus wanted the green light. He wanted the green light so much.

Then snow fell. It was a snowy day. Mom made a warm tent with her wings. Pip sat close.

“Jump,” said Pip. “I will catch you.”

Gus looked at the green light. Then he looked at Pip. He flapped his wings hard. He flew! He did not peek down. He landed by Pip.

“You did it!” said Pip.

Gus felt happy. The green light still glittered through the leaves. But Gus did not need it. He had his friend.

stories.text:
Mama said today Gus would fly. Gus sat in the nest and looked down. The ground was far. The wind was cold. Snow fell soft and white.

Then Gus saw the green light. It was at the back of a dark shop, glittering through the leaves. The green light was bright. The green light was far. Gus wanted the green light.

"Fly," said Mama.

Gus did not fly. Gus watched the green light. The green light, the green light. Snow got on his fluffy head. He did not care. He only wanted the green light.

A friend came. It was Pim the pigeon. "Come," said Pim. "I will help."

They went to the shop. Gus hid in a tent by the door. He took a peek. The green light was so close. It was still so far. Gus hopped. He flapped. He flew! He flew to the tree by the shop.

The green light glittered through the leaves. Gus could not reach it. But he could fly. Pim cheered. Mama cheered. Gus was happy. The green light stayed there, pretty and far, and Gus flew home through the snow.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: Come with Faye to the park. Rain falls on the pond. Plip, plip, plop. Faye is a duck. She loves the rain. It makes tiny rings on the water. She shakes her tail and does a happy wiggle. Her friend the frog hops by. "Ribbit! You look silly," says the frog. Faye laughs. "I am a wet duck," she says. She finds a rope on the grass. She pulls it. Splash! The rope was tied to a stick. Mud flies up. It lands on Faye's head. Now she is a muddy duck. The frog laughs so hard he falls in the pond. It is very funny. Faye swims and plays all day. The sun comes out. Far down the street, on a car, a green light pulses like a heartbeat. Faye sees it once. It is pretty. Then she looks away. She waddles home. Mud washes off. Rain is fun, but a warm bath is better. The moral is: play in the rain, but do not pull strange ropes.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Come with Faye to the pond on a sunny afternoon. She brings bread for the ducks. The rain from last night left big puddles. Faye likes puddles. She likes ducks more.

One duck waddles to her. His name is Bob. Bob is round and slow. Faye drops a crust. Bob tries to pick it up. He slips in the mud. He does a funny wiggle with his tail. Faye laughs out loud.

Then Faye sees a green light. It sits on a car parked far down the street. The green light pulses like a heartbeat. She wants to touch it. She takes one step. Then she stops.

A tiny piece of rope hangs from her pocket. Faye holds it. She looks at Bob. Bob is still hungry. The green light pulses again. She turns back to the pond.

Bob quacks for more bread. Faye gives him the last piece. The green light keeps pulsing far away. It will wait. Bob will not.

Some lights are only for looking. Friends are for feeding.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Came the rain, and Faye the duck was happy. She splashed in puddles on the sidewalk. She shook her tail and did a happy wiggle.

Then the sun came out. It was a sunny afternoon. Faye saw a green light on a car parked far down the street. The green light was pulsing like a heartbeat.

Faye stopped splashing. She wanted that green light. She reached for it with her tiny wings. She could not have it.

She tried to tie a rope to her wagon to get closer. The rope slipped. She fell in a puddle with a funny splash. A passing cat laughed.

Faye got up. She looked at the green light again. It was still pulsing like a heartbeat.

She walked toward it. The green light stayed far away. She kept turning back to it.

At last she sat down. The green light was just a light. She could not hold it.

Faye went back to her puddles. She wiggled her tail. Some things are nice to want, but puddles are nice to have.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Come see the duck in the rain. Faye watched it waddle down the sunny sidewalk. The duck did a happy wiggle. Rain fell from a sprinkler, not the sky. It was a funny joke of a storm. Faye laughed.

Then she saw the green light. It sat on a car parked far down the street. The green light pulsed like a heartbeat. Faye wanted it. She reached for it. The duck quacked. Faye did not hear.

She tied a rope to her wagon. She pulled it toward the green light. The duck followed, going wiggle, wiggle. But the car stayed far away. The green light pulsed like a heartbeat. Faye ran. The green light pulsed. She reached. The green light pulsed. Her tiny hands caught only air.

The duck sat down. It would not wiggle. Faye looked back. The duck was her real friend. The green light was just a light. She gave the duck a hug. Some lights we want but cannot hold. Friends we can. That is the true treasure.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Clouds ran away and the sun came out. Faye sat in the grass and watched a duck in the rain puddle. The duck went wiggle, wiggle, splash. Faye laughed. Then she saw the green light.

It sat on a car parked far down the street. The green light pulsed like a heartbeat. Faye stood up. She wanted it.

"Come back," said Faye to the duck. The duck did not come back. Faye did not care. She wanted the green light.

She found a rope. She tied a tiny loop. She threw it at the car. The rope fell down. She threw it again. Her shoe came off and landed in the puddle. The duck quacked at her shoe like it was a hat.

Faye did not care. She reached for the green light. It pulsed like a heartbeat. It was far down the street. It was always far down the street. Green light, green light, green light.

The duck walked home alone. Faye still reached. Some lights just want to be looked at, not held.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Papa gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Finn turned it over. Tiny seeds slid down inside. They made a soft sound. Like rain on a roof.

Finn took it outside. The wind blew hard. It was a windy morning. He sat by the muddy path. He shook the rainstick. The seeds went tick, tick, tick. The sound made him smile. It felt like a tickle in his ears.

A train went by far away. Whoo, whoo. Finn waved at the train. Then he saw something across the big field. A green light. It glowed like a lantern. It was small and far away. Finn watched it for a while.

He shook the rainstick again. Tick, tick, tick. The green light did not move. Finn stood up. He walked toward it. But the field was too big.

Then Mama called him home. Finn ran back. He hugged the rainstick. The twist? The green light was just the porch lamp on his own house. Finn laughed. He shook the rainstick all the way inside.

stories.name: Finn

stories.text:
Papa gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Finn turned it over. Tiny seeds slid inside. They made a soft sound, like rain. Finn liked that sound a lot.

That windy morning, Finn took the rainstick outside. He walked past the train tracks. The wind pushed his hair. The rainstick went shhh, shhh, shhh.

Then Finn saw the green light. It was far away, across a big field. It glowed like a lantern. The green light looked warm. Finn wished he could hold it. But the field was muddy. His boots went squish, squish.

Finn held up his rainstick. He shook it hard. The seeds went tickle, tickle inside. The green light seemed to blink at him. Finn smiled. He felt brave.

He took one big step into the mud. Then he heard a giggle. His little sister was hiding in the grass. She had a jar with a firefly inside. The green light was just her jar!

Finn laughed. He shook the rainstick for her. They sat in the muddy grass together. The rainstick made rain sounds. The firefly made a green light. It was a good morning.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
Papa gave Finn a rainstick. Finn held it up. The beads inside went shhh, shhh. It sounded like rain.

Finn sat by the window. Wind pushed the trees. The morning was gray and windy.

Then Finn saw it. Across the big field, the green light glowed like a lantern. It wobbled in the wind.

Finn took his rainstick and walked outside. The field was muddy. His boots went squish, squish.

He shook the rainstick. Shhh, shhh. The sound made him feel brave. He looked at the green light. It was still far away.

A train went by. Whoo, whoo. Finn waved, but the train did not stop.

He walked and walked. The wind made his ears tickle. The green light shone and shone. Finn wanted to hold it. He wanted it more than his rainstick.

Then Finn tripped. The rainstick flew up, up, up. It landed in the mud. Finn picked it up. The beads were stuck.

He shook it. No sound came out. He shook it again. Nothing.

Finn sat down in the wet grass. He looked across the field. The green light still glowed like a lantern.

Then Finn heard a tiny sound. Shhh, shhh. It was not his rainstick. It was real rain, falling soft on his head. The green light was just the sun, peeking through the clouds.

Finn smiled. He walked home to Papa, muddy boots and all.

stories.text:
Papa gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Finn turned it over. Little seeds slid down inside. They made a soft sound like rain.

Finn liked the rainstick. He took it everywhere. But when he shook it, he always looked out the window. Across the big field, far away, he saw the green light. It glowed like a lantern in the windy morning.

Finn put down the rainstick. He walked to the edge of the field. The grass was muddy. He could not cross. A train went by and blew its whistle. The wind made his coat flap.

He went back inside. He picked up the rainstick. Shake, shake. It did not tickle his ears like before. He looked for the green light again.

Shake, shake. Green light. Shake, shake. Green light. He thought of nothing else.

Then Mama came in. She smiled and took the rainstick. She turned it the other way. Out fell a tiny green bulb.

Finn laughed. The green light was in his hand all along.

features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Papa gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Finn turned it over. Tiny seeds fell inside. They made a soft sound like rain. Finn liked that sound.

Then Finn saw the green light. It was across a big field. It glowed like a lantern. The wind blew hard that windy morning. The grass waved. Finn wanted the green light. He wanted it so much.

"Stay here," Papa said. "The train is coming."

But Finn ran. He ran across the muddy field. His boots went squish. The wind tried to tickle his ears. He did not stop. He wanted the green light. Green light, green light, green light.

The green light stayed far away. It never got closer. Finn ran and ran. His breath came fast.

Then Finn stopped. He looked down. The rainstick was still in his hand. He turned it over. Seeds fell. Rain sound came out.

The green light was not a lantern. It was the sun on a wet rock. The rock did not want him. The rainstick did.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Great big waves rocked the little sailboat. Nate was a seal. He liked to ride his sailboat on windy mornings.

The wind blew hard. It was cold. Nate put on his red glove. He did not want to slide off the boat.

His friend Pip was a small bird. Pip sat on the sail. "Look over there," said Pip.

Nate looked. In the dark of the woods, something was glowing like a lantern. It was a green light.

Nate wanted to touch the green light. He swam to the shore. He slid on the rocks. He went into the trees. The green light stayed far away.

Pip flew to him. "The green light is too far," said Pip.

Nate looked once more. The green light blinked like a star. Then he went back to his sailboat with Pip. They sailed home together.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Great big waves rocked the little sailboat. Nate was a seal. He liked to ride the boat. The wind blew hard. It was a windy morning.

Nate saw a green light in the dark of the woods. It glowed like a lantern. He wanted to touch it.

"Come back!" said his friend Pip. Pip was a bird.

Nate slid off the boat. The water was cold. He put on his glove. He did not want the cold.

He swam to the woods. The green light was far away. He reached for it. It was too far.

Pip flew over. "Let's go back," Pip said.

They went back to the sailboat. The wind pushed them. Nate saw the green light again. It glowed like a lantern. He looked and looked.

The boat went fast. The green light got small. Then it was gone.

Nate was sad. Pip sat by him. "The green light is pretty," Pip said.

"Yes," said Nate. "But I can not have it."

They sailed home in the wind.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gulls called over the water where Nate swam. Nate was a seal. He loved a little sailboat with a red sail. Every windy morning, Nate raced the sailboat across the bay.

Then Nate saw something in the dark of the woods. A green light was glowing like a lantern. It was small and far away. Nate wanted to touch it.

“Come back,” said his friend Pim. Pim was a puffin. “The water is cold.”

Nate did not listen. He slid onto the rocks. He left one glove on the shore. He wanted the green light.

The wind blew hard. The sailboat sailed away without him. Nate climbed and slid, up and down. The green light stayed far.

“Please,” said Nate. “Just once.”

Pim pulled his flipper. “The boat is waiting.”

Nate looked back. The green light glowed like a lantern in the dark trees. He could not reach it. He never could.

So Nate slid back to the cold sea. He raced the sailboat again. But sometimes, on a windy morning, he still looked at the woods, and the green light, and wished.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gray morning wind pushed Nate's sailboat across the water. A seal popped up beside it. The seal said, "Hello, Nate." Nate waved his glove.

Then Nate saw the green light. It was far off in the dark of the woods. It glowed like a lantern. Nate forgot the seal. He forgot the sailboat.

"Come back," said the seal. But Nate slid the boat toward the trees.

The wind was cold. Nate held his glove up. The green light blinked. It was so pretty. It was so far.

The seal slid in close. "The woods are dark," she said.

"I want the green light," Nate said.

The seal pushed the boat back. The green light pulled it in. Back and forth went the boat.

Morning turned to noon. Nate's glove was wet. The green light stayed in the dark of the woods. It glowed like a lantern. Nate reached. He reached and reached.

"Stay with me," said the seal.

Nate looked at his friend. He looked at the green light.

The green light. Always the green light.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gulls cried over the water where Nate watched a seal and a sailboat. The boat rocked. The seal swam. Nate clapped his hands. Then he saw the green light.

It was in the dark of the woods, glowing like a lantern. The wind blew hard. It was a windy morning.

Nate put on his glove. He felt cold. He wanted the green light.

He tried to slide down the hill to the woods. His friend Ben came too. Ben helped him up. But the green light was far away.

Nate ran to the green light. The green light stayed far. The seal and the sailboat did not matter now. Only the green light.

He reached. He could not touch it. The green light glowed like a lantern in the dark trees.

He kept going. He got cold. Ben held his glove. But Nate only saw the green light. The green light. The green light.

He never got it. Ben walked him home.

The green light still glowed behind the trees. Nate still wanted it. The green light.

stories.text:
Little Tess met a snowflake that could talk. It landed on her mittens and said, "Hello, I am Flake." Tess laughed. She had never heard a snowflake speak.

Flake told her about the sky. He told her about the moon and the cold wind. He said he fell a long way to see the ground. Tess held him close so he would not melt. They walked to the hill.

The night was foggy and soft. Far off, on a tower, a green light shone. It looked pale and misty in the fog. Tess saw the green light and wished she could touch it. But the tower was too far. The green light stayed small and far away.

Flake said, "I can not go there. I am made of snow." Tess felt sad. She gave a soft tap to her mittens.

Then Flake said, "I must go now." He melted into one drop. The drop was heavy on her hand. Tess smiled. She knew he was not gone. He was just water now, and water can go anywhere.

stories.name: Tess

stories.text:
Little Tess met a snowflake that could talk. It landed on her mittens and said, "Hello, I am Pip." Tess laughed. She had never heard a snowflake talk before.

Pip told her about the sky. He told her about the moon. He told her how he fell past a tall tower on a foggy night. Tess liked Pip. She wanted to keep him.

Then Tess saw the green light. It was on a tower far away. The green light looked pale and misty in the fog. It called to her. She reached for it, but it was too far. She could not touch it.

Pip said, "I saw the green light too. It is always far away."

Tess felt a heavy feeling. She wanted the green light. She also wanted Pip to stay.

Then Pip began to melt. He got smaller and smaller. "Goodbye, Tess," he said.

Tess felt sad. She gave a soft tap on her mitten. But then she smiled. The puddle on her mitten was not water. It was a tiny new snowflake. Pip was back. And the green light still shone, pale and misty, on the far tower.

stories.text:
Little Tess met a snowflake that could talk. It landed on her mitton and said, "Hello, I am Flake." Tess laughed. She asked Flake where it came from. Flake said, "From the sky, near the moon."

That night was foggy. Tess looked out her window. Far away, on a tower, she saw a green light. It looked pale and misty in the fog. The green light was soft and far. She wanted to touch it.

"Can we go there?" Tess asked. Flake said, "No. That green light is too far."

Tess put on her coat. The fog felt heavy on her face. She took a step. Then she looked back at the green light. It was still there, pale and misty. She took another step. The green light pulled her.

"You can not reach it," Flake said. Tess did not listen. She walked and walked. Her boots went tap, tap, tap on the cold road. She kept her eyes on the green light.

Then Flake said, "Tess, look down." Tess looked. Her boots were not on the road. They were on a cloud. The twist was this: the tower was right under her feet, and the green light was only a lamp by her door.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Tess met a snowflake that could talk. It fell on her mitten and said, "Hello, I am Flake." Tess laughed. "You can talk!" Flake said, "Yes, and I can tap on your nose." It did a small tap. Tess giggled.

That night the fog came. The moon was shy and hid. Tess looked out her window. Far away, on a tower, she saw the green light. It was pale and misty. The green light pulled at her. "Come," it seemed to say.

"Look," said Flake. "Do not go."

But Tess thought of the green light. She wanted the green light. The fog felt heavy on the town. She wanted the green light. She wanted the green light. She could not stop wanting the green light.

Flake said, "I am not just a snowflake. I am the green light's small sister. It calls everyone. It is lonely. Do not go."

Tess blinked. The green light was just a light on a tower. She held Flake close. The moon came out. The fog went away. Tess did not go.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Tess met a talking snowflake in the fog. It landed on her mitten and said, "Hello, Tess." Tess jumped. Snow should not talk. But this snowflake did. It told her its name was Pip. Pip said he fell from a tall cloud. Tess laughed and asked him to stay. Then she saw the green light.

The green light was on a tower far away. It looked pale and misty in the foggy night. The moon was hidden. Tess wanted the green light. She wanted it more than Pip. "Do not go," said Pip. But Tess did not hear him.

She walked toward the green light. The fog was heavy. Her boots went tap, tap on the ice. She reached for the green light. The green light stayed far away. "Green light," she said. "Green light. Green light." Pip melted in her mitten. She did not feel him go.

Tess never touched the green light. But the small wet spot on her mitten began to shine. It was green. It was a tiny green light, and it was hers. She held it close and smiled.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
By the stove, Nina waited for the kettle to whistle. It was a hot summer day. The kitchen felt like a little oven. She held a soft cloth in her pocket.

Then the kettle sang. Nina took it off the fire. She poured the water for her tea. But she did not want tea. She wanted to go outside.

She went to the bridge over the river. The sun was high. The water was slow. Then she saw the green light on the bridge rail. It sparkled like a jewel. Nina wanted it. She reached for the green light. It was only sun on a wet stone. Her hand came back empty.

She did not run home. She sat down. The green light was just a trick of the day. Some pretty things are not for holding. Nina went back to her cold tea.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
By the stove, Nina waits for the kettle. It starts to whistle. Steam puffs up like a small cloud. Nina likes that sound.

She takes the kettle off. She pours tea for her mom. Then she goes outside. The day is hot. The sun is big.

Nina walks to the bridge over the river. She puts her hands in her pocket. She feels a soft wind.

Then she sees the green light. It sits far away on the water. It sparkles like a jewel. Nina wants to hold it.

She leans on the bridge. She reaches out. The green light stays far away. It always stays far away.

Nina tries to run to it. Her feet are hot. The green light does not come closer.

She goes home. The kettle is cold now. It does not whistle. Nina sits by the window. She thinks of the green light. She is sad. Some things you can see, but you can never hold.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text: Before breakfast, Nina put the kettle on. It began to whistle. The sound was high and happy. She loved that sound more than anything. Then she looked out the window. Far away, on the bridge over the river, she saw the green light. It sparkled like a jewel in the hot summer day. Nina forgot the kettle. She ran out the door. She ran down the hill. She ran to the bridge. The green light danced on the water. It was so pretty. She reached for it. Her hand touched only air. The green light stayed far away. Nina sat down. She felt a sad, soft ache in her chest. She put her hand in her pocket. There was nothing there. Not a coin. Not a wish. The kettle was still whistling at home, but she could not hear it now. She only saw the green light. She wanted it so much. But she could not have it. Some pretty things are only for looking, never for holding. Nina walked home alone.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text: By noon the kettle whistled on Nina's stove. She poured the hot water and watched the steam. It curled up like a small ghost. Then she put the kettle in her pocket of quiet and went outside. The summer day was very hot. She walked to the bridge over the river. There, far off, shone the green light. It sparkled like a jewel on the water. Nina wanted it. She wanted it more than her kettle. She reached out. The green light stayed far away. Every day she came back to the bridge. She would leave her kettle to whistle alone. She would run to the river. The green light always sparkled. It never came close. Her kettle grew cold at home. One soft evening she sat on the bridge and cried. She had chased the green light all summer. She had lost her warm tea. It is sad to want a thing you can never hold. That was the lesson Nina learned too late.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Boiling water made the kettle sing on the stove. Nina liked that sound. It was warm and soft, like a hug. She poured the water and made tea.

Then she saw the green light. It was on a bridge over the river. It sparkled like a jewel in the hot summer sun. Nina wanted to touch it.

She set down her cup and began to run. The kettle whistled behind her, but she did not stop.

The green light shone on the bridge. She reached for the green light. Her hand went through it. The green light was not real. It was only a trick of the sun on the water.

Nina sat down. She was sad. The green light was still there, sparkling like a jewel. She could not have it.

The kettle grew cold at home. The tea was never drunk.

Some things we want are only lights we can never hold.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone sat in Nina's hand. It never melted. It tasted like strawberries and stars.

Nina licked it once. Then she licked it twice. "This is the best cone in the world," she said.

Her friend Ben ran up. "Share it with me?"

"Only a little," said Nina. The cone was sticky and sweet.

The sun went down. It made the sky pink and gold. Then Nina saw a green light on a tower far away. It was round like a marble. It blinked once, slow and soft.

"What is that?" Nina asked.

"I don't know," said Ben. "Maybe a star that fell."

Nina held her cone up to peek at the green light. The green light did not come closer. It just glowed.

"Can we go there?" she said.

"It's too far," said Ben. "Eat your cone."

So Nina ate. The green light stayed on the tower. It was pretty. But her cone was sweeter.

"Okay," she said. "Let's go home."

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone can never melt. Nina got it at the fair. It was pink and cold and sweet.

"Lick it slow," said her friend Ben.

Nina licked it slow. The sun went down. The sky turned orange.

Then Nina saw a green light. It sat on a tower far away. The green light was round like a marble.

"Look," said Nina. "The green light."

"That is far," said Ben.

Nina held her cone. The green light blinked. It looked like a tiny mint. Her ice cream was sticky on her hand.

"I want to peek at it," said Nina.

"We can wave," said Ben.

They waved. The green light did not come closer. It just stayed on the tower.

Nina licked her cone again. It was still magic. It did not melt. But her eyes went back to the green light.

"Help me reach it," she said.

Ben held her hand. "We can try tomorrow."

The sun was gone. The green light stayed. Nina held her sticky cone and looked and looked.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text: A magic ice cream cone can make any wish come true. Nina found one in her yard. It was cold and sweet. "I wish for a big hat," she said. The cone did nothing. "Try a small wish," said her friend Ben. So Nina wished for a flower. A red flower grew by her shoe. "It works," said Ben. But then the sun went down. The sky turned pink and orange. Far away, on a tower, a green light blinked on. It looked round like a marble. Nina forgot her cone. "Look," she said. "The green light." She held up her sticky hand. The green light was so far away. "I wish to touch the green light," she said. The cone did not help. She wished again. Nothing. The green light just sat there on the tower. "You can't reach it," said Ben. "I want to," said Nina. She peeked at the green light until the sky went dark. Her cone melted in her hand.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone sat in Nina's hand. It was cold and sweet. It never melted, not even a drop. Nina licked it once. It tasted like pink.

"Look," said her friend Ben. "The sun is going down."

The sun was big and orange. It made the sky soft. Nina saw a tower far away. On the tower, a green light blinked on. It was round like a marble. It was small and far and bright.

"Wow," Nina said. "Do you see the green light?"

"Yes," said Ben. "But your ice cream is dripping."

Nina looked down. A sticky drop ran on her thumb. She licked it. Then she looked up again. The green light was still there. It was so pretty. Nina wanted to hold it.

"Come on," said Ben. "Let's go home."

Nina took one step. Then she stopped. She peeked at the tower again. The green light called to her. It was far, far away. She could not touch it. She could not have it. But she wanted it so much.

Ben took her hand. "The green light is too far," he said. "But your ice cream is right here."

Nina looked at the cone. Then she looked back at the green light. She held the cone tight. She walked home slow. The green light stayed on the tower. It always did.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone sat in Nina's hand. It was cold and sweet. It never melted. Nina licked it once.

Then she saw the green light.

The sun was going down. The green light sat on a tower far away. It was round like a marble. It glowed at sunset.

"Look," Nina said. "The green light."

Her friend Ben looked. "It is far away," he said.

Nina wanted the green light. She held her magic ice cream cone. It got sticky. She did not care.

"Come back," Ben said. "Your cone is dripping."

Nina reached for the green light. She could not touch it.

"Please," she said. "Please, green light."

The sun went down more. The green light peeked over the tower. It was still far.

Ben took her hand. "Stay here," he said.

Nina looked at the green light. She looked and looked.

"Green light," she whispered. "Green light."

Her magic ice cream cone melted away. She did not see. She only saw the green light.

Ben sat with her. The sky got dark. The green light stayed far away. Nina reached and reached. She could not have it.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
I like the playground slide. Leo climbs the little steps. He holds the rail with one glove. He is a bit shy at the top. Then he slides down fast. He laughs and claps. Again, again, again.

His mom sings a soft song. The park gets dark. Fog rolls in like a gray blanket. They walk home down the long road. Leo holds his mom's hand. The fog hides the trees.

Far away, at the end of the long road, Leo sees a green light. It is steady and still. It looks like a small moon on a pole. He does not ask about it. He just looks.

At home, Leo has warm milk. He draws the slide with a blue crayon. He draws himself on it, happy. Before bed, he peeks out the window. The green light is steady and still, far down the road.

Leo smiles. He is safe and warm. He did the big slide all by himself. That makes him brave. He sleeps well.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text: I love the tall slide at the playground. Leo climbs up the steps. He holds the rail with one glove. Then he slides down fast. Whee! He goes again and again. Soon it is dark. Fog comes in. Leo can see a green light at the end of a long road. It looks steady and still. He feels shy. He wants to go to it. But he stays on the slide. His mom calls, "Time to go." Leo does not want to leave. The green light stays far away. It does not move. He slides one more time. Then he walks home. He hears his mom sing a soft song. The green light is behind the fog now. Leo smiles. He will come back tomorrow. The slide is still his favorite.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
I like the big slide at the playground. Leo climbs the steps. He holds the rail with one glove. Down he goes, fast and happy.

But then the fog comes. The night gets soft and gray. Leo looks down the long road. Far away, the green light is there. It is steady and still. It does not move. It does not blink.

Leo slides again. He wants to sing. He is a shy boy, so he sings low. The green light stays at the end of the long road. Steady and still.

He goes up the steps. He goes down the slide. Up and down. The green light is always there. Steady and still.

His mom calls him home. Leo waves to the slide. He waves to the road. The green light is steady and still. He cannot reach it. That is okay.

At home, he is warm. He ate a good snack. He gets a big hug. He feels glad. The green light is far away. But Leo is happy.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
In the park, Leo climbs the slide. Up the steps. Down the slide. Up and down. He holds his red glove tight. The slide is fun. But then he sees it. At the end of a long road, the green light is steady and still. It is a foggy night.

Leo slides again. He wants to sing. But he feels shy. He looks at the slide. Then he looks at the green light. The slide is close. The green light is far.

He goes down once more. The green light is steady and still. He thinks, green light, green light, green light. He forgets the slide. He just wants the green light. It is a foggy night.

His mom calls him. Leo, come home. He holds his glove. He walks to her. She gives him a hug. The slide is still there. The green light is still there. But his mom is warm. He feels happy. The green light can wait.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
I like the playground slide. Leo climbs the steps. He holds the rail with one glove. Down he goes. Whee! The slide is fun.

Then Leo looks past the fence. Far away is a long road. At the end of the road is a green light. It is steady and still.

Leo wants the green light. He forgets the slide. Green light. Green light. He is shy, but he whispers, "Green light."

He walks down the long road. The night is foggy. The green light stays far away. Green light. Green light. His glove feels cold.

A dog comes. The dog does not sing. The dog just walks with Leo. Leo smiles.

The fog lifts a little. Leo sees his mom at the end of the road. She waves. The green light is still there, steady and still.

Leo runs to his mom. She hugs him. He does not need to reach the green light. He is warm. He is home. The slide can wait for tomorrow.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
One morning June went to the sea to fish. She put a worm on her hook. She waited and waited. Then she pulled up a boot. It was old and brown. A fish was inside the boot! June did not want the boot. She wanted a big fish for supper.

She looked across the town. On a roof, a green light was bobbing up and down. It looked small and far. June said, “I wish I had that green light.” But she could not reach it. She let her line swing in the water.

The sun came up. The sea was calm. June did not catch a fish. But she gave the boot a hug. It was not a fish. It was still a good day.

Sometimes we want what we cannot have. The little green light on the roof stayed far away. But June went home happy with her boot.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
One early morning, June the fisherman pulled up her net. Inside was a wet, old boot. "Not a fish," she said. She set the boot on the dock.

Then she saw the green light. It was on a roof across the town. It bobbed up and down in the cold air. June did not know why it was there. She wanted to touch it.

She rowed her boat toward the town. The water was smooth. She felt calm. But the green light kept bobbing. It was far away.

June stopped by a swing in a small park. She sat and watched the green light. She wished she could hug it close. But a light is not a thing to hold.

She went back to her dock. The boot was still there. She picked it up and smiled. Maybe a boot is not a fish. But it can still be useful.

The green light bobbed on. June could not reach it. That was okay.

Some things we want are far away. We can still be happy with what we have.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
One morning June the fisherman pulled up her net and found a boot inside. It was old and brown and full of mud. She did not want a boot. She wanted fish. She shook the boot and a small crab fell out. The crab ran to the water and was gone. June sat down and had a sip of tea.

Then she saw the green light. It was on a roof across the town. It was bobbing up and down in the early morning air. June wanted the green light. She could not have it. She was too far away.

She went back to her net. She found a sock. She found a can. She took a deep breath to stay calm. But the green light kept bobbing up and down in her head.

At noon she gave up and went home. Her little girl ran out and gave her a big hug. June told her about the boot. Her girl laughed and said, “Maybe the boot wanted a friend.”

June looked once more at the roof. The green light was still bobbing up and down. She let it swing in her mind, then let it go.

A thing you cannot reach can still teach you to love what you hold.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
O June went down to the dock to fish. She wanted a big fish for supper. Her boat went up and down on the water.

Then she saw a boot. It was old and brown. It floated by her boat. June pulled the boot out with her net. A boot is not a fish. June felt sad.

She looked across the town. On a roof, a green light was bobbing up and down. The green light was small and far. It was early morning. The green light went up, then down, then up. June wanted to touch the green light. She reached out her hand. She could not reach it.

The green light kept bobbing up and down. June forgot her boot. She forgot her fish. She only saw the green light. The green light, the green light, the green light.

The sun came up. The green light went away. June held her boot. She gave it a hug. The water was calm. She let the boot go. A boot is not a fish, but it can still make you smile.

stories.text: On a calm morning June went to the sea to fish. She pulled up her net. A boot was in it. June did not want a boot. She wanted a fish. Then she saw the green light. It was on a roof across the town. It was bobbing up and down. Green light. Green light. June forgot the boot. She forgot the fish. She forgot her boat. Green light. Green light. She let the net swing. She let the boot drop. She did not hug her warm coat. She just looked across the town. Green light. Green light. The sun came up. The green light stayed far away. June reached out her hand. She could not touch it. Green light. Green light. At last she sat down. The morning was calm. The green light was still on the roof. It was still bobbing up and down. June held her empty net. She said, a light you cannot hold is not yours. Want what you have.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Cara makes Tess laugh every day. Cara tells jokes at lunch. She tells jokes on the bus. Her jokes are silly, but Tess loves them.

One sunny afternoon, they sit on the steps. Cara holds an egg. She says, "Why did the egg cross the road?" Tess waits. Cara taps the egg on her knee. "To get to the other side!" The egg does not break. They laugh and laugh.

Then Tess looks down the street. A car sits far away. A green light flickers on and off on the car. On. Off. On. It is small and far. Tess watches it for a moment.

Cara says, "Are you sad?" Tess says, "A little." Cara says, "I know a joke about a sad girl." Tess smiles. Cara tells it. It is silly. Tess feels better.

The green light flickers on the car. Tess does not need to reach it. She has her friend. They go inside for a snack.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: Cracking jokes is what Mina does best. She tells one about a chicken and an egg. Tess laughs so hard she has to tap the table. It is a sunny afternoon, and they sit outside with cold drinks. Mina does a silly dance. Then she tells a joke about a sleepy bear. Tess feels happy. But down the street, a car is parked far away. On its roof, a green light flickers on and off. Tess stops laughing. She looks at the green light. It blinks like a slow wink. Mina sees her face. "Hey," Mina says. "Want another joke?" Tess nods. Mina tells one about a turtle who forgot his shell. Tess smiles again. The green light flickers on and off. She looks back at Mina. Mina taps her cup. "You are my best friend," Mina says. "Even when you drift away." Tess laughs. The green light flickers on and off, far down the sunny street. But Mina's jokes are closer. And that is better.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Cora tells the best jokes. Tess laughs so hard her tummy hurts. They sit on the porch steps in the sunny afternoon. Cora does a joke about an egg who learns to dance. Tess giggles and slaps her knee.

Then Tess looks down the street. A car sits far away. The green light flickers on and off, on and off. She wants to touch it. She does not know why.

"Hey," says Cora. "You went quiet."

"Just thinking," Tess says. She turns back to her friend. Cora tells a silly joke about a tap that drips a song. Tess laughs again.

But her eyes slide away. The green light flickers on and off. It is so far. It is so small. Cora gives her a little nudge.

"Stay with me," Cora says. "One more joke."

Tess nods. She taps her toes. The joke is about a cat who cannot sing. It is funny. For a moment Tess forgets.

Then she peeks again. The green light flickers on and off. Always there. Always far.

Cora holds her hand. "We can look later," she says. "Together."

Tess smiles. The green light flickers on and off, but her friend is here. That is enough for now.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Carl likes to tell jokes. Tess laughs at every one. He tells a joke about an egg. It is so silly. Tess holds her belly. She laughs and laughs.

Then Tess sees the green light. It is far down the street, on a car. The green light is flickering on and off. She stops laughing. She stares at the green light.

"Tess? You okay?" Carl asks.

"The green light," Tess says. "It is flickering."

She taps her foot. She wants to go to the green light. She wants to touch it. She wants it more than jokes. More than eggs. More than silly things.

Carl waves his hand. "Let's tell one more joke."

But Tess watches the green light. The green light flickers. The green light calls. She thinks green light, green light, green light.

Carl stays with her. He does not leave. That helps.

The sun is warm. The green light keeps flickering. Tess sighs. She stays. She stays with her friend.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: Cora tells the best jokes. She makes Tess laugh until her sides hurt. One joke was about an egg who wanted to be a dancer. Tess laughed so hard she had to tap the table. It was a sunny afternoon, and they sat on the porch. Then Tess saw it. Far down the street, on a car, the green light flickered on and off. She stopped laughing. Her eyes went wide. "Tess?" Cora said. "You okay?" But Tess was gone. The green light blinked. It was so far away. It was so silly to want it. But she wanted it. She wanted the green light. The green light. The green light. Cora tapped her arm. "Come on, laugh with me." Tess tried. She really tried. But all she could think was green light, green light, green light. Cora hugged her. "I'll help you," she said. "We can watch it together." So they did. They watched the green light flicker. And Cora told one more joke about a dancing egg. Tess laughed a little. The green light stayed far away. But Cora stayed close.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: in a tent across the camp
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
A plane flew high above Ravi's tent. He sat dry inside and made a paper kite. Rain tapped on the tent like a soft spoon on a cup.

Ravi wanted to fly his kite. But the sky was wet and gray. So he waited.

Across the camp, another tent glowed. A green light shone inside it. The green light looked pale and misty in the rain. Ravi watched the green light for a moment. Then he looked back at his kite.

He drew a round sun on the paper. He wanted warm days.

The rain stopped. Ravi ran outside. He let his kite dance up on the wind. It went up, up, up.

Then a gust took it. The kite flew far and landed near the tent with the green light.

A girl came out. She held his kite. "I saw it from my tent," she said. "It looks like a bird."

Ravi laughed. Now he had a friend to fly with. The green light was just a lamp. But the evening turned happy and bright.

He drops his kite string. The kite lifts up. It does a dance in the wind. The kite flies like a plane.

stories.text:
Small Kai was a kitten with wings. His wings were soft and gray. One cold autumn evening, he found a flower in the yard. It was a sparkly red flower. He tried to pull it from the ground. It would not come out.

Then Kai saw a green light. It was on a roof across the town. The green light was dim, like a sleepy eye. It blinked once. Kai forgot the flower.

He flew up high. The wind was cold. The green light stayed far away. He flew and flew. He could not reach it. The green light was always just ahead.

Kai went home. His wings were tired. The flower was still there. He did not pull it again.

Sometimes we want a green light we can never touch. But the small things near us are warm and real.

stories.name: Kai

stories.text:
Soft was the kitten with wings, and Kai held him close. The kitten purred like a little flower in the cold.

Autumn wind made Kai's coat feel thin. He walked to the edge of town. Across the roofs, far away, the green light blinked. It was dim, like a sleepy eye. The green light did not move.

Kai wanted to fly to it. He tried to stretch his own small wings. But the sky was too big. He sat down and watched the green light. A sparkly tear fell on his paw.

Each night he came back. The green light stayed across the town. It seemed to pull him, soft and slow. But his wings were small. The green light was far.

One evening the kitten with wings climbed onto Kai's shoulder. The kitten licked his ear. Kai felt warm again. He looked at the green light one last time.

Some lights are not for reaching. They are for loving from here.
